aiOverview.content: Vaccination is a safe and effective way to protect against serious, sometimes deadly, diseases by training your immune system to create antibodies without causing the illness itself. Vaccines are critical for public health, saving millions of lives annually and reducing the spread of infectious diseases. View all Key Vaccine Recommendations for 2025–2026 COVID-19: The CDC recommends an updated 2025–2026 COVID-19 vaccine for people ages 6 months and older to protect against severe illness, hospitalization, and death. The CDC recommends an updated 2025–2026 COVID-19 vaccine for people ages 6 months and older to protect against severe illness, hospitalization, and death CDC Flu (Influenza): An annual flu vaccine is recommended for everyone 6 months and older. RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus): Recommended for adults 75 and older, adults 50–74 with higher risk conditions, and pregnant people to protect infants. HPV (Human Papillomavirus): Routinely recommended for children aged 11–12, but available through age 26. Tdap/Td: Protects against tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (whooping cough). Shingles: The Shingrix vaccine is recommended for adults 50 and older. Common Childhood Vaccinations Routine childhood vaccines protect against diseases like measles, mumps, rubella (MMR), polio, varicella (chickenpox), and DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis). Babies (0–6 months): Initial doses of Hepatitis B, DTaP, Hib, Pneumococcal (PCV), Polio, and Rotavirus. 12–15 Months: MMR and Varicella doses are typically given in this range. 4–6 Years: Boosters for DTaP, Polio, MMR, and Varicella. 11–12 Years: Tdap, HPV, and Meningococcal vaccines. Vaccine Safety and Efficacy Side Effects: Mild side effects like headache, body aches, or a fever may occur, but they are normal signs that the body is building protection. Effectiveness: Routine child vaccinations (1994-2023) are estimated to have prevented 508 million illnesses and saved 1.1 million lives. Ingredients: Ingredients are thoroughly tested and serve to improve immunity (adjuvants), maintain safety (preservatives), and ensure stability. Vaccine Access and Scheduling Where to Get: Pharmacies (like CVS, Walgreens), healthcare provider offices, and health departments. Pharmacies (like CVS, Walgreens), healthcare provider offices, and health departments CVS , Walgreens), healthcare provider offices, and health departments Walgreens Records: It is important to keep a vaccination card and review immunization history at every health care visit. Travel: Specific vaccines may be necessary for international travel, which should be addressed 4-6 weeks before departure.
